modern:
For several days we’ve been thinking about the Savior’s passion, and for some time to come we’ll linger there. As we begin a new month, let’s seek the same longing for our Lord that glowed in the heart of the chosen bride. See how she leaps straight to *him*. There are no opening words; she doesn’t even mention his name. She’s in the heart of her subject at once, for she speaks of *him*, the only “him” in the world to her. How bold her love is! It was great condescension that let the weeping penitent anoint his feet with spikenard. It was rich love that let gentle Mary sit at his feet and learn from him. But here, love, strong, burning love, reaches for higher signs of his regard and closer signs of fellowship. Esther trembled in the presence of Ahasuerus, but the bride, in the joyful freedom of perfect love, knows no fear. If we’ve received the same free spirit, we can ask for the same thing.

By kisses we take her to mean all the different ways his love is shown, by which the believer is made to enjoy the love of Jesus. The kiss of *reconciliation* we enjoyed at our conversion, and it was as sweet as honey dripping from the comb. The kiss of *acceptance* is still warm on our forehead, as we know he has accepted us and our works through rich grace. The kiss of daily, present *fellowship* is what we long to have repeated day after day, until it turns into the kiss of *welcome*, which takes the soul from earth, and the kiss of *fulfillment*, which fills it with the joy of heaven. Faith is our walk, but fellowship we can feel is our rest. Faith is the road, but fellowship with Jesus is the well the pilgrim drinks from. O lover of our souls, don’t be a stranger to us. Let the lips of your blessing meet the lips of our asking. Let the lips of your fullness touch the lips of our need, and at once the kiss will be given.

modern:
This month of April is said to get its name from the Latin verb *aperio*, which means *to open*, because all the buds and blossoms are opening now, and we’ve reached the gates of the flowering year. Reader, if you aren’t saved yet, may your heart, in tune with the awakening of all nature, be opened to receive the Lord. Every blossoming flower warns you that *it is time to seek the Lord*. Don’t be out of tune with nature; let your heart bud and bloom with holy desires. Do you tell me the warm blood of youth is racing in your veins? Then I beg you, give your strength to the Lord. It was my unspeakable happiness to be called in early youth, and I could gladly praise the Lord every day for it. Salvation is priceless whenever it comes, but oh, an early salvation has double value. Young men and young women, since you may perish before you reach your prime, “*It is time to seek the Lord*.” You who feel the first signs of decline, hurry your steps. That hollow cough, that feverish flush, are warnings you mustn’t play with. For you *it is indeed time to seek the Lord*. Did I notice a little gray mixed in with your once thick hair? The years are creeping on fast, and death is coming nearer at a quick march. Let each return of spring stir you to set your house in order.

Dear reader, if you’re now well on in years, let me urge and beg you to delay no longer. There’s a day of grace for you now; be thankful for that. But it’s a limited time, and it grows shorter every time the clock ticks. Here in this silent room, on the first night of another month, I speak to you as best I can by paper and ink, and from my inmost soul, as God’s servant, I set this warning before you: “*It is time to seek the Lord*.” Don’t brush aside this word. It may be your last call away from destruction, the final syllable from the lips of grace.

modern:
He had never been slow to speak when he could bless people, but he wouldn’t say a single word for himself. “Never man spake like this man,” and never was anyone silent like him. Was this remarkable silence *the sign of his perfect self-sacrifice*? Did it show that he wouldn’t say a word to stop the slaughter of his sacred person, which he had dedicated as an offering for us? Had he given himself up so completely that he wouldn’t step in on his own behalf, even in the smallest way, but would be bound and killed as an unresisting, uncomplaining victim? Was this silence *a picture of how defenseless sin is*? Nothing can be said to lessen or excuse human guilt, and so he who bore its whole weight stood speechless before his judge.

Isn’t patient silence *the best answer to a world that argues back*? Calm endurance answers some questions far more convincingly than the loftiest eloquence. The best defenders of Christianity in the early days were its martyrs. The anvil breaks a crowd of hammers by quietly taking their blows. Didn’t the silent Lamb of God give us *a grand example of wisdom*? Where every word was an occasion for new blasphemy, the path of duty was to give no fuel to the flame of sin. The ambiguous and the false, the unworthy and the mean, will soon overthrow and disprove themselves, so the truth can afford to keep quiet, and finds silence to be its wisdom. Clearly, by his silence our Lord gave *a remarkable fulfillment of prophecy*. A long defense of himself would have gone against Isaiah’s prediction: “He is led as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.” By his quietness he proved beyond doubt that he was the true Lamb of God. As that, we greet him this morning. Be with us, Jesus, and in the silence of our hearts let us hear the voice of your love.

modern:
All of you who love the Lord, plead for this promise to be fulfilled soon. Praying is easy work when our desires are grounded and rooted in God’s own promise. How can the One who gave the word refuse to keep it? Unchanging truthfulness can’t lower itself to a lie, and eternal faithfulness can’t disgrace itself by neglect. God must bless his Son; his covenant binds him to it. What the Spirit moves us to ask for Jesus is what God has decreed to give him. Whenever you pray for the kingdom of Christ, let your eyes see the dawn of the blessed day that is drawing near, when the Crucified will be crowned in the very place where people rejected him. Take courage, you who work and toil prayerfully for Christ with only the smallest success. It won’t always be like this; better times are ahead of you. Your eyes can’t see the blissful future. Borrow the telescope of faith. Wipe the misty breath of your doubts from the glass. Look through it, and see the coming glory.

Reader, let us ask: *do you* make this your constant prayer? Remember that the same Christ who tells us to say, “Give us this day our daily bread,” had first given us this request: “Hallowed be thy name; Thy kingdom come; Thy will be done in earth as it is in heaven.” Don’t let your prayers all be about your own sins, your own needs, your own imperfections, your own trials. Let them climb the starry ladder and reach Christ himself. And then, as you come near the blood-sprinkled mercy seat, offer this prayer continually: “Lord, extend the kingdom of thy dear Son.” A request like that, offered earnestly, will lift the spirit of all your devotions. Make sure you prove your prayer is sincere by working to promote the Lord’s glory.

modern: He had been in agony all night. He had spent the early morning in the hall of Caiaphas. He had been rushed from Caiaphas to Pilate, from Pilate to Herod, and from Herod back to Pilate again. So he had very little strength left, and yet he was allowed neither food nor rest. They were eager for his blood, so they led him out to die, loaded with the cross. Oh, sorrowful procession! Well may the daughters of Jerusalem weep. My soul, weep too.

What do we learn here as we see our blessed Lord led out? Don’t we see the truth that was pictured in shadow by *the scapegoat*? Didn’t the high priest bring the scapegoat and put both his hands on its head, confessing the sins of the people, so that those sins would be laid on the goat and taken away from the people? Then the goat was led away into the wilderness by a man appointed for the task, and it carried away the sins of the people, so that if anyone looked for them, they couldn’t be found. Now we see Jesus brought before the priests and rulers, who pronounce him guilty. God himself charges our sins *to him*: “the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all”; “He was made sin for us.” And as the substitute for our guilt, carrying our sin on his shoulders, pictured by the cross, we see the great Scapegoat led away by the appointed officers of justice.

Dear friend, can you feel sure that he carried *your* sin? As you look at the cross on his shoulders, does it stand for *your* sin? There’s one way you can tell whether he carried your sin or not. Have you laid your hand on his head, confessed your sin and trusted in him? Then your sin doesn’t lie on you. It has all been transferred to Christ by blessed imputation, and he carries it on his shoulder as a load heavier than the cross.
Don’t let the picture fade until you’ve rejoiced in your own deliverance and worshiped the loving Redeemer on whom your sins were laid.

modern:
Here is a confession of sin *common* to all God’s chosen people. They have all fallen, and so in one chorus they all say, from the first who entered heaven to the last who will enter it, “All we like sheep have gone astray.” While the confession is united like this, it is also *individual* and particular: “We have turned every one to his own way.” There’s a special sinfulness in every single one of them. All are sinful, but each one with some particular aggravation not found in the others. It’s the mark of real repentance that while it naturally joins with other penitents, it also takes a place of its own, alone. “We have turned every one to his own way” is a confession that each person sinned against light given to them in particular, or sinned with an aggravation they couldn’t see in others. This confession is *without reserve*. There’s not a word to weaken its force, not a syllable of excuse. The confession is *a giving up of every plea of self-righteousness*. It’s the statement of people who know they are guilty, guilty with aggravations, guilty without excuse. They stand with their weapons of rebellion broken in pieces and cry, “All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way.”

Yet we hear no sorrowful wailing with this confession of sin, because the next sentence almost turns it into a song: “The Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.” It’s the most painful sentence of the three, but it overflows with comfort. It’s a strange thing that where misery was gathered together, mercy reigned; where sorrow reached its height, weary souls find rest. The bruised Savior is the healing of bruised hearts. See how the lowliest repentance gives way to confident assurance, simply by looking at Christ on the cross!

modern:
Grieving Christian, why are you weeping? Are you grieving over your own sinful desires? Look to your perfect Lord, and remember, you are complete in him. In God’s sight you’re as perfect as if you had never sinned. No, more than that: the Lord our Righteousness has put a divine robe on you, so that you have more than human righteousness. You have the righteousness of God. You who are grieving because of the sin and corruption you were born with, remember, none of your sins can condemn you. You’ve learned to hate sin, but you’ve also learned that sin is not yours: it was laid on Christ’s head. Your standing isn’t in yourself; it’s in Christ. Your acceptance isn’t in yourself, but in your Lord. You’re as fully accepted by God today, with all your sinfulness, as you will be when you stand before his throne, free from all corruption. Oh, I beg you, take hold of this precious thought: *perfection in Christ*! For you are “complete in him.” With your Savior’s robe on, you are as holy as the Holy One. “Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us.”

Christian, let your heart rejoice, for you are “accepted in the beloved.” What do you have to fear? Let your face always wear a smile. Live close to your Master. Live in the suburbs of the Celestial City. For soon, when your time comes, you’ll rise up to where your Jesus sits and reign at his right hand. And all this because the divine Lord “was made to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”

modern:
It does our souls great good to rise above this present evil world to something nobler and better. The cares of this world and the deceitfulness of riches tend to choke everything good in us, and we grow irritable, discouraged, perhaps proud and worldly. It’s good for us to cut down these thorns and briers, because heavenly seed sown among them isn’t likely to give a harvest. And where will we find a better sickle to cut them down with than fellowship with God and the things of the kingdom? In the valleys of Switzerland many of the people are deformed, and all look sickly, because the air is full of foul vapors and is close and stagnant. But up on the mountain you find a hardy race who breathe the clear, fresh air as it blows from the untouched snows of the Alpine peaks. It would be good if the people of the valley could often leave their homes among the marshes and the fever mists and breathe the bracing air on the hills.

This evening I invite you to a climb like that. May the Spirit of God help us leave the mists of fear and the fevers of worry, and all the ills that gather in this valley of earth, and climb the mountains of joy and blessedness we look forward to. May God the Holy Spirit cut the cords that keep us here below, and help us rise! Too often we sit like chained eagles fastened to the rock, except that, unlike the eagle, we start to love our chain, and perhaps, if it really came to it, we’d be unwilling to have it snapped. May God give us grace now, if we can’t escape the chain as to our bodies, at least to escape it in our spirits. And leaving the body at the foot of the hill, like a servant, may our soul, like Abraham, reach the top of the mountain, to enjoy fellowship with the Most High there.

modern: In Simon’s carrying the cross we see a picture of the church’s work in every generation: she is the cross-bearer behind Jesus. Notice, then, Christian: Jesus doesn’t suffer in a way that rules out your suffering. He carries a cross, not so that you can escape it, but so that you can endure it. Christ frees you from sin, but not from sorrow. Remember that, and expect to suffer.

But let’s comfort ourselves with this thought: in our case, as in Simon’s, *it isn’t our cross but Christ’s cross that we carry.* When you’re harassed for your godliness, when your faith brings the trial of cruel mockings on you, remember it isn’t *your* cross; it’s *Christ’s* cross. And how delightful it is to carry the cross of our Lord Jesus!

*You carry the cross behind him.* You have blessed company; your path is marked with your Lord’s footprints. The mark of his blood-red shoulder is on that heavy load. It’s *his* cross, and he goes ahead of you as a shepherd goes ahead of his sheep. Take up your cross daily and follow him.

Don’t forget, either, *that you carry this cross in partnership*. Some think Simon only carried one end of the cross, not the whole of it. That’s very possible. Christ may have carried the heavier part, where the crossbeam is, and Simon may have carried the lighter end. Certainly that’s how it is with you: you only carry the light end of the cross; Christ carried the heavier end.

And remember, *though Simon only had to carry the cross for a very little while, it gave him lasting honor*. In the same way, the cross *we* carry is only for a little while at most, and then we’ll receive the crown, the glory. Surely we should love the cross, and instead of shrinking from it, *count it very dear*, when it works out for us “a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory.”

modern:
Humbling the soul always *brings a real blessing with it*. If we empty our hearts of self, God will fill them with his love. Whoever wants close fellowship with Christ should remember the word of the Lord: “To this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word.” Stoop if you want to climb to heaven. Don’t we say of Jesus, “He descended that he might ascend”? So must you. You must grow downward so that you can grow upward, because the sweetest fellowship with heaven is had by humble souls, and by them alone. God will refuse no blessing to a thoroughly humbled spirit. “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” with all its riches and treasures. God’s whole treasury will be signed over by deed of gift to the soul that is humble enough to receive it without growing proud because of it.

God blesses us all right up to the full limit of what is safe for him to do. If you don’t get a blessing, it’s because it isn’t safe for you to have one. If our heavenly Father let your unhumbled spirit win a victory in his holy war, you would steal the crown for yourself, and when you met a fresh enemy, you’d fall victim to him. So you’re kept low for your own safety. When someone is sincerely humble, and never dares to touch so much as a grain of the praise, there’s hardly any limit to what God will do for him. Humility makes us ready to be blessed by the God of all grace, and fits us to deal well with our fellow men. True humility is a flower that will beautify any garden. It’s a sauce you can season every dish of life with, and you’ll find it improves every one. Whether it’s prayer or praise, work or suffering, you can’t use too much of the genuine salt of humility.

modern:
Jesus, carrying his cross, went out to suffer outside the gate. The Christian’s reason for leaving the camp of the world’s sin and religion isn’t that he loves to be different, but that *Jesus did*, and the disciple must follow his Master. Christ was “not of the world.” His life and his witness were a constant protest against fitting in with the world. There was never such overflowing love for people as you find in him, but still he was separate from sinners. In the same way Christ’s people must “go forth unto him.” They must take their stand “without the camp,” as witnesses for the truth. They must be ready to walk the straight and narrow path. They must have bold, unflinching, lion-like hearts, loving Christ first and his truth next, and Christ and his truth above all the world.

Jesus wants his people to “go forth without the camp” *so that they may be made holy*. You can’t grow in grace to any great degree while you’re conformed to the world. The life of separation may be a path of sorrow, but it’s the highway of safety. And though the separated life may cost you many pangs and make every day a battle, it’s a happy life after all. No joy can beat that of the soldier of Christ. Jesus shows himself so graciously, and gives such sweet refreshment, that the soldier feels more calm and peace in his daily fight than others do in their hours of rest. The highway of holiness is the highway of fellowship. This is how we can hope *to win the crown*, if divine grace enables us to follow Christ faithfully “without the camp.” The crown of glory will follow the cross of separation. A moment’s shame will be well repaid by eternal honor. A little while of bearing witness will seem nothing when we are “for ever with the Lord.”

modern: By his death our Lord Jesus didn’t buy the right to only part of us, but to the whole person. In his suffering he had in view making us holy through and through, spirit, soul and body, so that in this threefold kingdom he himself might reign supreme without a rival. It’s the job of the new nature God has given the born-again to assert the rights of the Lord Jesus Christ. My soul, as far as you are a child of God, you must conquer all the rest of yourself that is still unblessed. You must bring all your powers and passions under the silver scepter of Jesus’ gracious reign, and you must never be satisfied until he who is King by purchase also becomes King by gracious coronation and reigns in you supreme. Since sin has no right to any part of us, then, we’re fighting a good and lawful war when we try, in the name of God, to drive it out. O my body, you are a member of Christ: shall I put up with you being under the prince of darkness? O my soul, Christ has suffered for your sins and redeemed you with his most precious blood: shall I let your memory become a storehouse of evil, or your passions firebrands of wickedness? Shall I hand over my judgment to be twisted by error, or my will to be led in chains of sin? No, my soul, you are Christ’s, and sin has no right to you.

Take courage about this, Christian! Don’t be disheartened, as though your spiritual enemies could never be destroyed. You are able to overcome them, not in your own strength (the weakest of them would be too much for you that way), but you can and will overcome them through the blood of the Lamb. Don’t ask, “How shall I dispossess them, for they are greater and mightier than I?” But go to the Strong One for strength, wait humbly on God, and the mighty God of Jacob will surely come to the rescue, and you will sing of victory through his grace.

modern: One instructive writer has made a sad list of the honors the blinded people of Israel gave their long-awaited King.

1. They gave him *a procession of honor*, in which Roman soldiers, Jewish priests, men and women all took part, while he himself carried his cross. This is the triumph the world gives the One who comes to overthrow humanity’s worst enemies. Mocking shouts are his only cheers, and cruel taunts his only songs of praise.

2. They presented him with *the wine of honor*. Instead of a golden cup of fine wine, they offered him the criminal’s drugged death drink. He refused it, because he wanted to keep his senses clear to taste death. And afterward, when he cried, “I thirst,” they gave him vinegar mixed with gall, pushed to his mouth on a sponge. Oh, wretched, hateful hospitality to the King’s Son!

3. He was given *a guard of honor*, who showed their respect for him by gambling over his clothes, which they had taken as their loot. Such was the bodyguard of the One heaven adores: a squad of four brutal gamblers.

4. *A throne of honor* was found for him on the bloody tree. Rebel men would give their rightful Lord no easier place to rest. The cross was really the full expression of the world’s feeling toward him. “There,” they seemed to say, “you Son of God, this is how God himself should be treated, if we could reach him.”

5. *The title of honor* was in name “King of the Jews,” but the blinded nation flatly rejected that, and really called him “King of thieves,” by choosing Barabbas over him and putting Jesus in the place of greatest shame between two thieves. So in every way his glory was turned into shame by the sons of men, but it will yet gladden the eyes of saints and angels, world without end.

modern: In this *solemn confession* it’s good to notice that David plainly names his sin. He doesn’t call it manslaughter, or speak of it as a lapse that led to an unfortunate accident happening to a good man. He calls it by its true name: bloodguiltiness. He didn’t actually kill Bathsheba’s husband, but it was planned in David’s heart that Uriah should be killed, and before the Lord he was his murderer. Learn to be honest with God in confession. Don’t give fair names to foul sins; call them what you like, they won’t smell any sweeter. What God sees them to be, you work at feeling them to be, and with complete openness of heart admit what they really are. Notice that David was clearly weighed down by how hateful his sin was. It’s easy to use words, but hard to feel what they mean. The fifty-first Psalm is the photograph of a crushed spirit. Let’s seek the same brokenness of heart, because however fine our words may be, if our heart isn’t aware that sin deserves hell, we can’t expect to find forgiveness.

Our text has in it *an earnest prayer*. It’s addressed to the God of *salvation*. It’s his right to forgive; it’s his very name and office to save those who seek his face. Better still, the text calls him the God of *my* salvation. Yes, blessed be his name, while I am still coming to him through Jesus’ blood, I can rejoice in the God of *my* salvation.

The psalmist ends with *a worthy vow*: if God will deliver him, he will *sing*. No, more, he will “*sing aloud*.” Who could sing in any other way about a mercy like this! But notice the subject of the song: “*Thy righteousness*.” We must sing of the finished work of a precious Savior, and whoever knows most of forgiving love will sing the loudest.

modern:
Among the various explanations of this thought-provoking question, this one is full of teaching: “If the innocent substitute for sinners, suffer thus, what will be done when the sinner himself—the dry tree—shall fall into the hands of an angry God?” When God saw Jesus in the sinner’s place, he didn’t spare him; and when he finds the unregenerate without Christ, he won’t spare them. O sinner, Jesus was led away by his enemies: so you will be dragged away by demons to the place appointed for you. Jesus was deserted by God; and if he, who was a sinner only by imputation, was deserted, how much more will you be? “*Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani*?” What an awful cry! But what will your cry be when you say, “O God! O God! why hast thou forsaken me?” and the answer comes back, “Because ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof: I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when your fear cometh.” If God didn’t spare his own Son, how much less will he spare you! What whips of burning wire will be yours when conscience strikes you with all its terrors!

You richest, merriest, most self-righteous sinners, who would stand in your place when God says, “Awake, O sword, against the man that rejected me; smite him, and let him feel the smart for ever?” Jesus was spat on: sinner, what shame will be yours! We can’t sum up in one word the whole mass of sorrows that came together on the head of Jesus, who died for us, so it’s impossible for us to tell you what streams, what oceans of grief must roll over *your* spirit if you die as you are now. You may die like that; you may die now. By the agonies of Christ, by his wounds and by his blood, don’t bring the wrath to come upon yourselves! Trust in the Son of God, and you will never die.

modern:
See how independent of outward circumstances the Holy Spirit can make the Christian! What a bright light can shine within us when everything is dark outside! How firm, how happy, how calm, how peaceful we can be when the world shakes back and forth and the pillars of the earth are removed! Even death itself, with all its terrible influences, has no power to stop the music of a Christian’s heart. It makes that music sweeter, clearer, more heavenly, until the last kind thing death can do is let the earthly song melt into the heavenly chorus, the passing joy into eternal bliss! So let’s trust the blessed Spirit’s power to comfort us.

Dear reader, are you facing poverty? Don’t be afraid. The divine Spirit can give you, in your need, more plenty than the rich have in their abundance. You don’t know what joys may be stored up for you in the cottage around which grace will plant the roses of contentment. Are you aware that your bodily strength is failing more and more? Do you expect to suffer long nights of weakness and days of pain? Oh, don’t be sad! That bed may become a throne to you. You have little idea how every pang that shoots through your body may be a refining fire to burn up your dross, a beam of glory to light up the hidden parts of your soul. Are your eyes growing dim? Jesus will be your light. Are your ears failing? Jesus’ name will be your soul’s best music, and his person your dear delight. Socrates used to say, “Philosophers can be happy without music”; and Christians can be happier than philosophers when every outward reason for rejoicing is taken away. In you, my God, my heart will triumph, whatever troubles come from outside! By your power, O blessed Spirit, my heart will be exceedingly glad, though everything here below should fail me.

modern: In the rowdy mob that hounded the Redeemer to his death, there were some gracious souls whose bitter anguish found an outlet in wailing and lament, fitting music for that march of sorrow. When my soul can see in imagination the Savior carrying his cross to Calvary, she joins the godly women and weeps with them. And there truly is reason to grieve, a reason deeper than those mourning women thought. They grieved over innocence mistreated, goodness persecuted, love bleeding, meekness about to die. But my heart has a deeper and more bitter reason to mourn. My sins were the whips that tore those blessed shoulders and crowned that bleeding forehead with thorns. My sins cried, “Crucify him! crucify him!” and laid the cross on his gracious shoulders. His being led out to die is sorrow enough for one eternity, but my having been his murderer is more grief, infinitely more, than one poor fountain of tears can express.

It isn’t hard to guess why those women loved and wept, but they couldn’t have had greater reasons for love and grief than my heart has. The widow of Nain saw her son given back to her, but I myself have been raised to new life. Peter’s mother-in-law was cured of a fever, but I of the greater plague of sin. Seven devils were cast out of Mary Magdalene, but a whole legion out of me. Mary and Martha were favored with visits, but he lives with me. His mother carried his body, but he is formed in me, the hope of glory. Since I’m no less in debt than the holy women, let me be no less grateful or sorrowful.

modern:
These words can be translated, “thy *goodness* hath made me great.” David gratefully credited all his greatness not to his own goodness, but to the goodness of God. “Thy *providence*” is another reading, and providence is simply goodness in action. Goodness is the bud and providence the flower; or goodness is the seed and providence the harvest. Some translate it, “thy *help*,” which is just another word for providence, since providence is the firm ally of the saints, helping them in the service of their Lord. Or again, “thy *humility* hath made me great.” “Thy *condescension*” might serve as a reading that takes in all of these ideas, including *humility*. It’s God making himself small that makes us great. We’re so small that if God showed his greatness without stooping, we’d be trampled under his feet. But God, who must stoop to view the skies and bow down to see what angels do, turns his eye lower still, looks on the lowly and contrite, and makes them great.

There are still other readings. The Septuagint, for instance, reads, “thy discipline”—thy fatherly correction—“hath made me great”; while the Chaldee paraphrase reads, “thy word hath increased me.” Still the idea is the same. David credits all his own greatness to the stooping goodness of his Father in heaven. May this thought echo in our hearts this evening as we lay our crowns at Jesus’ feet and cry, “thy gentleness hath made me great.” How wonderful our experience of God’s gentleness has been! How gentle his corrections have been! How gentle his patience! How gentle his teaching! How gentle his drawing of us! Think about this, believer. Let gratitude be awakened; let humility be deepened; let love be stirred to life before you fall asleep tonight.

modern: The hill of comfort is the hill of Calvary. The house of consolation is built with the wood of the cross. The temple of heavenly blessing is founded on the split rock, split by the spear that pierced his side. No scene in sacred history ever gladdens the soul like the tragedy of Calvary.

Light springs from the midday midnight of Golgotha, and every plant of the field blooms sweetly under the shadow of the once cursed tree. In that place of thirst, grace has dug a fountain that keeps gushing with water as pure as crystal, each drop able to ease the sorrows of humanity. You who have had your times of struggle will admit that it wasn’t on the Mount of Olives that you found comfort, nor on Sinai, nor on Tabor, but that Gethsemane, Gabbatha and Golgotha have been a source of comfort to you. The bitter herbs of Gethsemane have often taken away the bitterness of your life. The scourge of Gabbatha has often whipped your worries away, and the groans of Calvary give us rare and rich comfort. We’d never have known Christ’s love in all its heights and depths if he hadn’t died; nor could we guess the Father’s deep love if he hadn’t given his Son to die. The everyday mercies we enjoy all sing of love, just as a seashell held to your ear whispers of the deep sea it came from. But if we want to hear the ocean itself, we mustn’t look at everyday blessings, but at the events of the crucifixion. Whoever wants to know love, let them go to Calvary and see the Man of sorrows die.

modern: Storm and long darkness, along with the immediate danger of shipwreck, had left the ship’s crew in a sad state. Only one man among them stayed perfectly calm, and by his word the rest were reassured. Paul was the only one with heart enough to say, “Sirs, be of good cheer.” There were veteran Roman soldiers on board, and brave old sailors, and yet their poor Jewish prisoner had more spirit than all of them. He had a secret Friend who kept his courage up. The Lord Jesus had sent a heavenly messenger to whisper words of comfort in his faithful servant’s ear, and so his face shone and he spoke like a man at ease.

If we fear the Lord, we can look for him to step in just in time when our case is at its worst. Storms don’t keep angels from us, and darkness doesn’t hold them back. Seraphs don’t think it beneath them to visit the poorest of the heavenly family. If angels’ visits are few and far between at ordinary times, they’ll be frequent in our nights of storm and tossing. Friends may drop away from us when we’re under pressure, but our fellowship with the inhabitants of the angelic world will be all the richer; and in the strength of love-words brought to us from the throne by way of Jacob’s ladder, we’ll be strong to do great deeds. Dear reader, is this an hour of distress for you? Then ask for special help. Jesus is the angel of the covenant, and if his presence is earnestly sought now, it won’t be refused. Those who, like Paul, have had the angel of God standing by them on a night of storm, when anchors would no longer hold and rocks were near, remember what heart-cheer that presence brings.

modern: Did earth or heaven ever see a sadder sight of sorrow! In soul and body our Lord felt as weak as water poured out on the ground. The dropping of the cross into its socket had shaken him violently, strained every ligament, pained every nerve and more or less dislocated all his bones. Weighed down by his own weight, the majestic sufferer felt the strain grow every moment of those six long hours. His sense of faintness and weakness was overwhelming, while to his own awareness he became nothing but a mass of misery and swooning sickness. When Daniel saw the great vision, this is how he describes what he felt: “There remained no strength in me, for my vigour was turned into corruption, and I retained no strength.” How much fainter must our greater Prophet have been when he saw the dreadful vision of the wrath of God and felt it in his own soul! For us, feelings like those our Lord endured would have been unbearable, and kind unconsciousness would have come to our rescue. But in his case, he was wounded and *felt* the sword; he drained the cup and *tasted* every drop.

As we kneel before the throne of our now ascended Savior, let’s remember well the way by which he prepared it as a throne of grace for us. Let’s drink of his cup in spirit, so that we may be strengthened for our own hour of heaviness whenever it comes. In his natural body every part suffered, and so it must be in his spiritual body. But just as his body came out of all its griefs and sorrows unharmed, into glory and power, so his spiritual body will come through the furnace without even the smell of fire on it.

modern: It’s good for us when prayers about our sorrows are linked with pleas about our sins: when, being under God’s hand, we aren’t wholly taken up with our pain, but remember our offenses against God. It’s good, too, to take both sorrow and sin to the same place. It was to God that David carried his sorrow; it was to God that David confessed his sin. Notice, then, *we must take our sorrows to God*. Even your little sorrows you can roll onto God, for he counts the hairs of your head; and your great sorrows you can hand over to him, for he holds the ocean in the hollow of his hand. Go to him, whatever your present trouble is, and you’ll find him able and willing to relieve you. *But we must take our sins to God too*. We must carry them to the cross, so that the blood may fall on them, to wash away their guilt and destroy their defiling power.

The special lesson of the text is this: *we are to go to the Lord with sorrows and with sins in the right spirit*. Notice that all David asks about his sorrow is, “*Look upon* mine affliction and my pain”; but the next request is far more direct, definite, decided and plain: “*Forgive* all my sins.” Many sufferers would have put it, “Remove my affliction and my pain, and look at my sins.” But David doesn’t say that. He cries, “Lord, as for my affliction and my pain, I won’t dictate to your wisdom. Lord, look at them; I’ll leave them to you. I’d be glad to have my pain taken away, but do as you will. But as for my sins, Lord, I know what I want done with them: I must have them forgiven. I can’t bear to lie under their curse for a moment.” A Christian counts sorrow lighter on the scales than sin. He can bear his troubles continuing, but he can’t carry the burden of his sins.

modern:
Our blessed Lord went through a terrible sinking and melting of soul. “The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity, but a wounded spirit who can bear?” Deep depression of spirit is the most painful of all trials; everything else is nothing beside it. No wonder the suffering Savior cried to his God, “Be not far from me,” for more than at any other time, a person needs God when his heart is melted within him with heaviness. Believer, come near the cross this morning and humbly worship the King of glory as one who was once brought far lower in mental distress and inner anguish than any of us. And notice how fit he is to be a faithful High Priest who can be touched with the feeling of our weaknesses. Especially those of us whose sadness comes straight from losing the felt sense of our Father’s love should enter into close and intimate fellowship with Jesus. Let’s not give way to despair, since the Master has passed through this dark room ahead of us. Our souls may sometimes long and faint, and thirst to the point of anguish, to see the light of the Lord’s face. At such times let’s steady ourselves with the sweet fact of our great High Priest’s sympathy. Our drops of sorrow may well be forgotten in the ocean of his griefs; but how high our love ought to rise!

Come in, O strong and deep love of Jesus, like the sea at the flood of the spring tides. Cover all my powers, drown all my sins, wash away all my cares, lift up my earth-bound soul and float it right up to my Lord’s feet. And there let me lie, a poor broken shell washed up by his love, with no worth or value of my own, only daring to whisper to him that if he will put his ear to me, he’ll hear in my heart faint echoes of the vast waves of his own love, which have brought me where it is my delight to lie, at his feet forever.

modern: Nehemiah’s mention of the king’s garden brings to mind the *paradise* the King of kings prepared for Adam. Sin has completely ruined that lovely home of every delight, and driven the children of men out to work the ground, which produces thorns and briers for them. My soul, remember the fall, for it was *your* fall. Weep much because the Lord of love was so shamefully mistreated by the head of the human race, of which you are a member, as undeserving as any. See how dragons and demons live on this lovely earth, which was once a garden of delights.

Look over there at another King’s garden, which the King waters with his bloody sweat: *Gethsemane*, whose bitter herbs are far sweeter to renewed souls than even Eden’s luscious fruits. There the mischief of the serpent in the first garden was undone. There the curse was lifted from the earth and carried by the woman’s promised seed. My soul, think much about the agony and the passion. Go often to the garden of the olive press, and see your great Redeemer rescuing you from your lost condition. This truly is the garden of gardens, where the soul can see the guilt of sin and the power of love, two sights that surpass all others.

Is there no other King’s garden? Yes, *my heart*, you are one, or should be. How are the flowers doing? Is there any choice fruit showing? Does the King walk in it and rest in the arbors of my spirit? Let me see that the plants are trimmed and watered, and the mischievous foxes hunted out. Come, Lord, and let the heavenly wind blow at your coming, so that the spices of your garden may flow out. And I mustn’t forget the King’s garden of *the church*. O Lord, make it prosper. Rebuild her walls, nourish her plants, ripen her fruits, and reclaim the barren waste from the vast wilderness, and make it “a King’s garden.”

modern:
Myrrh may well be chosen as a picture of Jesus because of *its preciousness, its perfume, its pleasantness, its healing, preserving and disinfecting qualities, and its connection with sacrifice*. But why is he compared to “a *bundle* of myrrh”? First, for *plenty*. He isn’t a drop of it; he’s a whole box full. He isn’t a sprig or flower of it, but a whole bundle. There’s enough in Christ for all my needs; let me not be slow to make use of him. Our well-beloved is compared to a “bundle” again, for *variety*. There’s not only the one thing needful in Christ, but “in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily”: everything needful is in him. Take Jesus in his different roles, and you’ll see a marvelous variety: Prophet, Priest, King, Husband, Friend, Shepherd. Think of him in his life, death, resurrection, ascension and second coming. Look at him in his goodness, gentleness, courage, self-denial, love, faithfulness, truth and righteousness: everywhere he’s a bundle of preciousness.

He’s a “bundle of myrrh” for *keeping*: not loose myrrh to be dropped on the floor or stepped on, but myrrh tied up, myrrh to be stored in a box. We must value him as our best treasure. We must prize his words and his ordinances, and we must keep our thoughts of him and our knowledge of him as if under lock and key, in case the devil steals anything from us. What’s more, Jesus is a “bundle of myrrh” *for specialness*. The picture suggests God’s distinguishing, discriminating grace. From before the foundation of the world he was set apart for his people, and he gives out his perfume only to those who know how to enter into fellowship with him, to have close dealings with him. Oh, blessed people, whom the Lord has let into his secrets, and for whom he sets himself apart! Oh, choice and happy ones, who are made to say, “A bundle of myrrh is my well-beloved unto me.”

modern:
Our Lord’s being made “sin for us” is pictured here by the very meaningful transfer of sin to the bull, which the elders of the people carried out. Laying on the hand wasn’t just a touch, because in some other places of Scripture the original word means leaning heavily, as in the words, “thy wrath lieth hard upon me” ([[Ps.88.7|Psalm 88:7]]). Surely this is the very heart and nature of faith, which doesn’t only bring us into contact with the great Substitute, but teaches us to lean on him with the whole burden of our guilt. Jehovah made all the offenses of his covenant people meet on the head of the Substitute; but each one of the chosen is brought personally to sign this solemn covenant act, when by grace he is enabled to lay his hand by faith on the head of the “Lamb slain from before the foundation of the world.”

Believer, do you remember that thrilling day when you first knew you were pardoned through Jesus the sin-bearer? Can’t you gladly confess it and join with the writer in saying, “My soul recalls her day of deliverance with delight. Laden with guilt and full of fears, I saw my Saviour as my Substitute, and I laid my hand upon him; oh! how timidly at first, but courage grew and confidence was confirmed until I leaned my soul entirely upon him; and now it is my unceasing joy to know that my sins are no longer imputed to me, but laid on him, and like the debts of the wounded traveller, Jesus, like the good Samaritan, has said of all my future sinfulness, ‘Set that to my account.’” What a blessed discovery! modern:
Mockery was a large part of our Lord’s suffering. Judas mocked him in the garden. The chief priests and scribes laughed him to scorn. Herod treated him with contempt. The servants and the soldiers jeered at him and brutally insulted him. Pilate and his guards ridiculed his kingship. And on the cross all sorts of horrible jokes and hideous taunts were hurled at him. Ridicule is always hard to bear, but when we’re in intense pain it’s so heartless, so cruel, that it cuts us to the quick. Imagine the Savior crucified, racked with anguish far beyond anything we mortals can guess, and then picture that mixed crowd all wagging their heads or pushing out their lips in bitter contempt of one poor suffering victim! Surely there must have been something more in the crucified One than they could see, or such a great and mixed crowd wouldn’t all have honored him with such contempt. Wasn’t it evil admitting, at the very moment of its greatest seeming triumph, that after all it could do no more than mock the victorious goodness that was then reigning on the cross?

O Jesus, “despised and rejected of men,” how could you die for people who treated you so badly? Here is amazing love, divine love, yes, love beyond measure. We too despised you in the days before we were born again, and even since our new birth we’ve set the world high in our hearts. And yet you bleed to heal our wounds and die to give us life. Oh, that we could set you on a glorious high throne in every human heart! We would ring out your praises over land and sea, until people adored you as universally as they once all rejected you.

modern:
*It is well with the righteous always.* If it had said, “Say ye to the righteous, that it is well with him in his prosperity,” we would have had to be thankful for so great a gift, because prosperity is a dangerous time, and it’s a gift from heaven to be kept safe from its traps. Or if it had been written, “It is well with him when under persecution,” we would have had to be thankful for such a sustaining promise, because persecution is hard to bear. But when no time is mentioned, all time is included. God’s “shalls” must always be understood in their widest sense. From the beginning of the year to the end of the year, from the first gathering of evening shadows until the morning star shines, in every condition and in every circumstance, it will be well with the righteous.

It’s so well with him that we couldn’t imagine it being better. He’s *well fed*: he feeds on the flesh and blood of Jesus. He’s *well clothed*: he wears the imputed righteousness of Christ. He’s *well housed*: he lives in God. He’s *well married*: his soul is joined in the bonds of marriage to Christ. He’s *well provided for*: the Lord is his Shepherd. He’s *well endowed*: heaven is his inheritance. It is well with the righteous, *well on divine authority*: the mouth of God speaks the comforting promise. Dear friend, if God declares that all is well, ten thousand devils may declare it’s bad, but we laugh them all to scorn. Blessed be God for a faith that lets us believe God when his creatures contradict him. The Word says it is well with you at all times, righteous one. So, dear friend, if you can’t see it, let God’s word serve you instead of sight. Yes, believe it on divine authority more confidently than if your eyes and your feelings told you. Those God blesses are blessed indeed, and what his lips declare is truth most sure and steadfast.

modern: Here we see the Savior in the depth of his sorrows. No other place shows the griefs of Christ as well as Calvary, and no other moment at Calvary is as full of agony as the one when his cry tears the air: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” At that moment, physical weakness was joined with sharp mental torture from the shame and disgrace he had to go through. And to bring his grief to its terrible peak, he suffered spiritual agony beyond all words, from the withdrawal of his Father’s presence. This was the black midnight of his horror; this was when he went down into the abyss of suffering. No one can enter into the full meaning of these words. Some of us think at times that *we* could cry, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” There are times when the brightness of our Father’s smile is eclipsed by clouds and darkness. But let’s remember that God never really forsakes us. With us it’s only a seeming forsaking, but in Christ’s case it was real. We grieve at a little withdrawal of our Father’s love; but the real turning away of God’s face from his Son, who can measure how deep the agony was that it caused him?

In our case, the cry is often prompted by unbelief; in his case, it was the statement of a dreadful fact, for God had really turned away from him for a time. You poor, distressed soul, who once lived in the sunshine of God’s face but are now in darkness, remember that he hasn’t really forsaken you. God in the clouds is as much our God as when he shines out in all the brightness of his grace. But since even the *thought* that he has forsaken us gives us agony, what must the Savior’s sorrow have been when he cried, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”

modern:
*God’s people need lifting up.* By nature they are very heavy. They have no wings, or if they do, they’re like the dove of old that lay among the pots, and they need God’s grace to make them rise on wings covered with silver and feathers of yellow gold. By nature sparks fly upward, but the sinful souls of men fall downward. O Lord, “lift them up for ever!” David himself said, “Unto thee, O God, do I lift up my soul,” and here he feels the need for other people’s souls to be lifted up as well as his own. When you ask this blessing for yourself, don’t forget to seek it for others too.

There are three ways God’s people need to be lifted up. *They need to be raised in character.* Lift them up, O Lord; don’t let your people be like the people of the world! The world lies in the wicked one; lift them out of it! The people of the world are after silver and gold, chasing their own pleasures and the satisfying of their lusts. But Lord, lift your people above all this. Keep them from being “muck-rakers,” as John Bunyan calls the man who was always scraping after gold! Set their hearts on their risen Lord and their heavenly inheritance! Also, *believers need to be prospered in battle*. In the fight, if they seem to fall, O Lord, be pleased to give them the victory. If the enemy’s foot is on their necks for a moment, help them grab the sword of the Spirit and win the battle in the end. Lord, lift up your children’s spirits in the day of battle; don’t let them sit in the dust, mourning forever. Don’t let the enemy torment them badly and make them fret. But if, like Hannah, they’ve been persecuted, let them sing of the mercy of a God who rescues.
We can also ask our Lord to *lift them up at the last*! Lift them up by taking them home; lift their bodies from the grave, and raise their souls to your eternal kingdom in glory.

modern:
Standing at the foot of the cross, we see hands and feet and side all pouring out crimson streams of precious blood. It’s “precious” because of its power to *redeem* and *atone*. By it the sins of Christ’s people are atoned for. They are redeemed from under the law. They are reconciled to God, made one with him. Christ’s blood is also “precious” in its *cleansing power*: it “cleanseth from all sin.” “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.” Through Jesus’ blood not one spot is left on any believer, no wrinkle or any such thing. O precious blood, which makes us clean, removing the stains of so much sin, and lets us stand accepted in the Beloved, in spite of the many ways we’ve rebelled against our God!

Christ’s blood is also “precious” in its *preserving power*. We’re safe from the destroying angel under the sprinkled blood. Remember, it’s *God’s seeing* the blood that is the real reason we’re spared. Here’s comfort for us when the eye of faith is dim, for God’s eye is still the same. Christ’s blood is “precious” too in its *power to make us holy*. The same blood that justifies us by taking away sin goes on afterward to bring the new nature to life, and to lead it on to conquer sin and carry out God’s commands. There’s no motive for holiness as great as the one that streams from Jesus’ veins. And this blood is “precious,” unspeakably precious, because it has *overcoming power*. It is written, “They overcame through the blood of the Lamb.” How could they do anything else? Whoever fights with the precious blood of Jesus fights with a weapon that can’t know defeat. The blood of Jesus! Sin dies in its presence; death stops being death; heaven’s gates are opened. The blood of Jesus! We’ll march on, conquering and to conquer, as long as we can trust its power!

modern: Moses’ prayer was so mighty that everything depended on it. Moses’ requests did more to defeat the enemy than Joshua’s fighting. Yet both were needed. No, in the soul’s battle, force and fervor, decision and devotion, courage and intensity must join forces, and all will be well. You must wrestle with your sin, but most of the wrestling must be done alone, in private with God. Prayer, like Moses’, holds up the sign of the covenant before the Lord. The rod was the emblem of God’s working through Moses, the symbol of God’s rule in Israel. Learn, pleading saint, to hold up God’s promise and oath before him. The Lord can’t deny his own declarations. Hold up the rod of promise, and have what you want.

Moses grew tired, and then his friends helped him. Whenever your prayer flags, let faith hold up one hand and holy hope lift the other, and prayer, sitting on the Stone of Israel, the rock of our salvation, will keep on and prevail. Beware of growing faint in devotion; if Moses felt it, who can escape it? It’s far easier to fight sin in public than to pray against it in private. It’s been noticed that Joshua never grew tired of the fighting, but Moses did grow tired of the praying. The more spiritual an exercise is, the harder it is for flesh and blood to keep it up. So let’s cry for special strength, and may the Spirit of God, who helps our weaknesses, as he gave help to Moses, enable us like him to keep our hands steady “*until the going down of the sun*”: until the evening of life is over, until we come to the rising of a better sun, in the land where prayer is swallowed up in praise.

modern:
Reader, have *you* come to the blood of sprinkling? The question isn’t whether you’ve come to a knowledge of doctrine, or the keeping of ceremonies, or a certain kind of experience, but *have you come to the blood of Jesus*? The blood of Jesus is the life of all living godliness. If you’ve truly come to Jesus, we know how you came: the Holy Spirit sweetly brought you there. You came to the blood of sprinkling with no merits of your own. Guilty, lost and helpless, you came to take that blood, and that blood alone, as your everlasting hope. You came to the cross of Christ with a trembling, aching heart; and oh, what a precious sound it was to you to hear the voice of the blood of Jesus! The dropping of his blood is like the music of heaven to the repentant children of earth. We’re full of sin, but the Savior tells us to lift our eyes to him, and as we gaze at his streaming wounds, every drop of blood cries as it falls, “It is finished; I have made an end of sin; I have brought in everlasting righteousness.” Oh, sweet language of the precious blood of Jesus!

If you’ve come to that blood once, you’ll come to it constantly. Your life will be “Looking unto Jesus.” Your whole conduct will be summed up in this: “To whom coming.” Not to whom I *have* come, but to whom I am *always coming*. If you’ve ever come to the blood of sprinkling, you’ll feel your need to come to it every day. Anyone who doesn’t want to wash in it *every day* has never washed in it at all. The believer always feels it his joy and privilege that there is still a fountain opened. Past experiences are doubtful food for Christians; only a present coming to Christ can give us joy and comfort. This morning let’s sprinkle our doorposts fresh with blood, and then feast on the Lamb, sure that the destroying angel must pass us by.

modern: The worldly person’s cry is always, “Who will show us any good?” He looks for satisfaction in earthly comforts, pleasures and riches. But the sinner God has made alive knows only one good. “O that I knew where I might find *Him*!” When he’s truly awakened to feel his guilt, if you could pour the gold of India at his feet, he’d say, “Take it away: I want to find *Him*.” It’s a blessed thing for a person when all his desires are brought to a focus, so that they all center on one object. When he has fifty different desires, his heart is like a pond of stagnant water spread out into a marsh, breeding foul air and disease. But when all his desires are brought into one channel, his heart becomes like a river of pure water, running swiftly to water the fields. Happy is the one who has one desire, if that one desire is set on Christ, even if it hasn’t been satisfied yet. If Jesus is a soul’s desire, it’s a blessed sign of God’s work within. A person like that will never be content with mere ordinances. He’ll say, “I want Christ; I *must* have him. Mere ordinances are no use to me; I want *him*. Don’t offer me these. You’re offering me the empty pitcher while I’m dying of thirst. Give me water, or I’ll die. Jesus is my soul’s desire. I would see Jesus!”

Is this your condition right now, dear reader? Do you have only one desire, and is it for Christ? Then you aren’t far from the kingdom of heaven. Do you have only one wish in your heart, and is that one wish to be washed from all your sins in Jesus’ blood? Can you really say, “I would give all I have to be a Christian; I would give up everything I have and hope for, if I might but feel that I have an interest in Christ”? Then, despite all your fears, be of good cheer. The Lord loves you, and you’ll soon come out into daylight and rejoice in the freedom with which Christ makes people free.

modern: Rahab depended for her safety on the promise of the spies, whom she saw as representatives of the God of Israel. Her faith was simple and firm, but it was also very obedient. Tying the scarlet cord in the window was a very small act in itself, but she didn’t dare risk leaving it out. Come, my soul, isn’t there a lesson here for you? Have you paid attention to all your Lord’s will, even where some of his commands might seem unimportant? Have you kept, in his own way, the two ordinances of believers’ baptism and the Lord’s Supper? Neglecting these points to a great deal of unloving disobedience in your heart. From now on be blameless in everything, even down to tying a thread, if that is what is commanded.

This act of Rahab teaches a still more solemn lesson. Have I trusted completely in the precious blood of Jesus? Have I tied the scarlet cord in my window as if with a Gordian knot, so that my trust can never be removed? Or can I look out toward the Dead Sea of my sins, or the Jerusalem of my hopes, without seeing the blood, and seeing everything in connection with its blessed power? Anyone passing by can see a cord of such a striking color if it hangs from the window. It will be good for me if my life makes the power of the atonement plain to everyone watching. What is there to be ashamed of? Let people or devils stare if they want to; the blood is my boast and my song. My soul, there is One who will see that scarlet cord even when weak faith keeps you from seeing it yourself: Jehovah, the Avenger, will see it and pass over you. Jericho’s walls fell flat. Rahab’s house was on the wall, and yet it stood unmoved. My nature is built into the wall of humanity, and yet when destruction strikes the human race, I’ll be safe. My soul, tie the scarlet thread in the window again, and rest in peace.

modern:
When Jacob was on the far side of the brook Jabbok, and Esau was coming with armed men, he earnestly sought God’s protection, and as his chief argument he pleaded, “And thou saidst, I will surely do thee good.” Oh, the force of that plea! He was holding God to his word: “Thou saidst.” God’s faithfulness is a splendid horn of the altar to take hold of; but the promise, which has that faithfulness in it and something more besides, is a still mightier handhold: “Thou saidst, I will surely do thee good.” And has *he* said it, and won’t he do it? “Let God be true, and every man a liar.” Won’t *he* be true? Won’t *he* keep his word? Won’t every word that comes out of his lips stand firm and be fulfilled? Solomon used this same mighty plea at the opening of the temple. He pleaded with God to remember the word he had spoken to his father David, and to bless that place.

When someone gives a written promise to pay, his honor is at stake. He signs his name, and he must pay up when the time comes, or he loses his credit. It will never be said that God fails to honor his bills. The credit of the Most High has never been called into question, and never will be. He is punctual to the moment: he’s never early, but he’s never late. Search God’s word through, compare it with the experience of God’s people, and you’ll find that the two match from first to last. Many a white-haired patriarch has said with Joshua, “Not one thing hath failed of all the good things which the Lord your God spake concerning you; all are come to pass.” If you have a divine promise, you don’t need to plead it with an “if”; you can press it with certainty. The Lord meant to keep the promise, or he wouldn’t have given it. God doesn’t give his words just to quiet us and keep us hopeful for a while, meaning to put us off in the end. When he speaks, it’s because he means to do what he has said.

modern:
It was no small miracle to tear so strong and thick a curtain, but it wasn’t meant only as a show of power. It teaches us many lessons. *The old law of ordinances was put away*, and like a worn-out garment, torn and laid aside. When Jesus died, the sacrifices were all finished, because they were all fulfilled in him; and so the place where they were offered was marked with a clear sign of decay. That tear also *revealed all the hidden things of the old dispensation*. The mercy seat could now be seen, and the glory of God shone out above it. By the death of our Lord Jesus we have a clear revelation of God, for he was “not as Moses, who put a veil over his face.” Life and immortality are now brought to light, and things hidden since the foundation of the world are made plain in him.

*The yearly ceremony of atonement was abolished in this way.* The atoning blood that was once sprinkled behind the curtain every year has now been offered once for all by the great High Priest, and so the place of the symbolic rite was broken open. No blood of bulls or lambs is needed now, for Jesus has entered behind the curtain with his own blood. So *access to God is now allowed*, and it’s the privilege of every believer in Christ Jesus. It isn’t a small gap laid open for us to peer at the mercy seat through; the tear reaches from top to bottom. We may come boldly to the throne of heavenly grace. Would we be wrong to say that the opening of the Holy of Holies in this marvelous way at our Lord’s dying cry was *a picture of the opening of the gates of paradise* to all the saints because of his suffering? Our bleeding Lord has the key of heaven; he opens and no one shuts. Let’s go in with him into the heavenly places and sit with him there, until our common enemies are made his footstool.

modern: The word *Amen* solemnly confirms what came before it, and Jesus is the great Confirmer. Unchanging, he is forever “the Amen” in all *his promises*. *Sinner*, I’d like to comfort you with this thought. Jesus Christ said, “Come unto me all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” If you come to him, he’ll say “Amen” in your soul; his promise will be true *for you*. In the days of his flesh he said, “The bruised reed I will not break.” You poor, broken, bruised heart, if you come to him, he’ll say “Amen” to you, and it will be as true in *your* soul as in hundreds of cases in years gone by. *Christian*, isn’t this very comforting for you too: that not one word has gone out of the Savior’s lips that he has ever taken back? The words of Jesus will stand when heaven and earth pass away. If you get hold of even half a promise, you’ll find it true. Beware of the one called “Clip-promise,” who will destroy much of the comfort of God’s word.

Jesus is Yes and Amen in all *his offices*. He was a Priest to pardon and cleanse once; he is Amen as Priest still. He was a King to rule and reign for his people, and to defend them with his mighty arm; he is an Amen King, the same still. He was a Prophet of old, to foretell good things to come; his lips are most sweet and still drip with honey; he is an Amen Prophet. He is Amen in the merit of his blood; he is Amen in his righteousness. That sacred robe will stay most fair and glorious when nature decays. He is Amen in every single title he bears: your Husband, never seeking a divorce; your Friend, sticking closer than a brother; your Shepherd, with you in death’s dark valley; your Help and your Deliverer; your Castle and your High Tower; the Horn of your strength, your confidence, your joy, your all in all, and your Yes and Amen in all.

modern:
Child of God, death has lost its sting, because the devil’s power over it has been destroyed. So stop being afraid of dying. Ask God the Holy Spirit for grace, so that by knowing your Redeemer’s death closely and believing in it firmly, you may be strengthened for that dreaded hour. Living near the cross of Calvary, you can think of death with pleasure, and welcome it with intense delight when it comes. It’s sweet to die in the Lord; it’s a covenant blessing to sleep in Jesus. Death is no longer banishment; it’s a return from exile, a going home to the many mansions where the loved ones already live. The distance between the glorified spirits in heaven and the saints still fighting on earth seems great, but it isn’t. We aren’t far from home; a moment will bring us there.

The sail is spread; the soul is launched on the deep. How long will its voyage be? How many wearing winds must beat on the sail before it is furled in the harbor of peace? How long will that soul be tossed on the waves before it reaches the sea that knows no storm? Listen to the answer: “Absent from the body, present with the Lord.” That ship has only just left, but it’s already in harbor. It only spread its sail, and it was there. Like that ship long ago on the Lake of Galilee: a storm had tossed it, but Jesus said, “Peace, be still,” and *immediately* it came to land. Don’t think there’s a long gap between the moment of death and the eternity of glory. When the eyes close on earth, they open in heaven. The horses of fire aren’t on the road for an instant. So, child of God, what is there for you to fear in death, since through the death of your Lord its curse and sting are destroyed? Now it’s only a Jacob’s ladder, whose foot is in the dark grave but whose top reaches to everlasting glory.

modern: The sacramental army of God’s chosen is still fighting on earth, with Jesus Christ as the Captain of their salvation. He has said, “Lo! I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.” Listen to the shouts of war! Now let the people of God stand firm in their ranks, and let no one’s heart fail. It’s true that just now in England the battle is going against us, and unless the Lord Jesus lifts his sword, we don’t know what may become of the church of God in this land. But let’s be of good courage and play the man. There was never a day when Protestantism seemed to hang in the balance more than now, when a fierce effort is being made to restore the Roman antichrist to his old seat. We badly need a bold voice and a strong hand to preach and publish the old gospel that martyrs bled for and confessors died for. The Savior is still on earth by his Spirit; let that cheer us. He’s always in the thick of the fight, so the battle isn’t in doubt. And as the battle rages, what sweet satisfaction it is to know that the Lord Jesus, in his office as our great Intercessor, is pleading successfully for his people! Anxious onlooker, don’t look so much at the battle below, for there you’ll be wrapped in smoke and bewildered by garments rolled in blood. Lift your eyes up there, where the Savior lives and pleads, for while he intercedes, the cause of God is safe. Let’s fight as if everything depended on us, but let’s look up and know that everything depends on him.

Now, by the lilies of Christian purity, and by the roses of the Savior’s atonement, by the roes and by the hinds of the field, we charge you who love Jesus to fight bravely in the holy war, for truth and righteousness, for the kingdom and the crown jewels of your Master. Onward! “for the battle is not yours but God’s.”

modern:
The heart of Job’s comfort lies in that little word “My”: “My Redeemer”; and in the fact that the Redeemer lives. Oh, to get hold of a living Christ! We have to own a share in him before we can enjoy him. What good to me is gold in the mine? People are beggars in Peru and beg their bread in California. It’s gold in my purse that will meet my needs, by buying the bread I need. In the same way, a Redeemer who doesn’t redeem *me*, an avenger who will never stand up for *my* blood, what use would he be? Don’t rest content until by faith you can say, “Yes, I cast myself upon my living Lord; and he is mine.” It may be that you hold him with a feeble hand. You half think it’s presumptuous to say, “He lives as *my* Redeemer.” Yet remember, if you have even faith as a grain of mustard seed, that little faith *entitles* you to say it.

But there’s another word here too, expressing Job’s strong confidence: “*I know*.” To say, “I hope so, I trust so,” is comforting, and there are thousands in the fold of Jesus who hardly ever get much further. But to reach the very heart of comfort, you must say, “I know.” Ifs, buts and perhapses are sure murderers of peace and comfort. Doubts are dreary things in times of sorrow. Like wasps, they sting the soul! If I have any suspicion that Christ isn’t mine, then there’s vinegar mixed with the gall of death. But if I know that Jesus lives for me, then darkness isn’t dark: even the night is light around me. Surely if Job, in those ages before Christ came, could say, “I know,” *we* shouldn’t speak less positively. God forbid that our positiveness should be presumption. Let’s make sure our evidences are sound, so that we don’t build on an ungrounded hope. And then let’s not be satisfied with only the foundation, because it’s from the upper rooms that we get the widest view. A living Redeemer, truly mine, is joy unspeakable.

modern: He who was once despised and rejected by men now holds the place of honor as a dearly loved and honored Son. God’s right hand is *the place of majesty and favor*. Our Lord Jesus is his people’s representative. When he died for them, they had rest. He rose again for them, and they had freedom. When he sat down at his Father’s right hand, they had favor and honor and dignity. Christ’s being raised and lifted up is the lifting up, the acceptance, the enthroning and the glorifying of all his people, because he is their head and representative. So this sitting at God’s right hand is to be seen as the acceptance of the person of the Surety, the welcoming of the Representative, and therefore the acceptance of *our* souls. O saint, see in this your sure freedom from condemnation. “Who is he that condemneth?” Who will condemn the people who are in Jesus at the right hand of God?

The right hand is *the place of power*. Christ at God’s right hand has all power in heaven and on earth. Who will fight against a people whose Captain holds such power? O my soul, what can destroy you if Almighty Power is your helper? If the shield of the Almighty covers you, what sword can strike you? Rest secure. If Jesus is your all-prevailing King, and has trampled your enemies under his feet, if sin, death and hell are all conquered by him, and you are represented in him, you can’t possibly be destroyed.

modern:
Jesus our Lord, once crucified, dead and buried, now sits on the throne of glory. The highest place heaven offers is his by undisputed right. It’s sweet to remember that Christ’s exaltation in heaven is a *representative exaltation*. He is exalted at the Father’s right hand, and though as Jehovah he had surpassing glories that finite creatures can’t share, yet as the Mediator, the honors Jesus wears in heaven are the inheritance of all the saints. It’s delightful to think how close Christ’s union with his people is. We really are one with him; we are members of his body; and his exaltation is our exaltation. He will let us sit on his throne, just as he has overcome and sat down with his Father on his throne. He has a crown, and he gives us crowns too. He has a throne, but he isn’t content to have a throne to himself: at his right hand there must be his queen, dressed in “gold of Ophir.” He can’t be glorified without his bride.

Look up to Jesus now, believer. Let the eye of your faith see him with many crowns on his head, and remember that you’ll be like him one day, when you see him as he is. You won’t be as great as he is; you won’t be divine as he is; but still you’ll share in some measure the same honors, and enjoy the same happiness and the same dignity he has. Be content to live unknown for a little while, and to walk your weary way through the fields of poverty or up the hills of affliction, because before long you’ll reign with Christ, for he has “made us kings and priests unto God, and we shall reign for ever and ever.” Oh, what a wonderful thought for the children of God! We have Christ as our glorious representative in heaven’s courts *now*, and soon he’ll come and take us to himself, to be with him there, to see his glory and to share his joy.

modern:
What is this terror? It may be the cry of “Fire!”, or the noise of burglars, or imagined ghosts, or the shriek of sudden illness or death. We live in a world of death and sorrow, so we can expect trouble in the watches of the night as well as under the glare of the blazing sun. But this shouldn’t alarm us, because whatever the terror may be, the promise is that the believer won’t be afraid. Why should he be? Let’s put it more closely: why should *we* be? God our Father is here, and will be here all through the lonely hours. He is an almighty Watcher, a sleepless Guardian, a faithful Friend. Nothing can happen without his direction, for even hell itself is under his control. Darkness isn’t dark to him. He has promised to be a wall of fire around his people, and who can break through a barrier like that? Worldly people may well be afraid, for they have an angry God above them, a guilty conscience within them and a gaping hell beneath them. But we who rest in Jesus are saved from all of these through rich mercy.

If we give way to foolish fear, we’ll dishonor the faith we profess and lead others to doubt that godliness is real. We ought to be afraid of being afraid, in case we grieve the Holy Spirit by foolish distrust. Down, then, you gloomy forebodings and groundless fears! God hasn’t forgotten to be gracious, or shut up his tender mercies. It may be night in the soul, but there’s no need for terror, for the God of love doesn’t change. Children of light may walk in darkness, but that doesn’t mean they’re cast away. No, now they’re able to prove they are God’s children by trusting their heavenly Father in a way hypocrites can’t.

modern:
We go to Christ for forgiveness, and then too often look to the law for power to fight our sins. Paul rebukes us for this: “O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you, that ye should not obey the truth? This only would I learn of you, Received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith? are ye so foolish? having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?” Take your sins to Christ’s cross, because the old self can only be crucified there: we are crucified *with him*. The only weapon to fight sin with is the spear that pierced Jesus’ side.

To give an example: you want to overcome a bad temper; how do you go about it? It’s very possible you’ve never tried the right way, going to Jesus with it. How did I get salvation? I came to Jesus just as I was, and I trusted him to save me. Must I kill my bad temper the same way? It’s the only way I can ever kill it. I must go to the cross with it and say to Jesus, “Lord, I trust thee to deliver me from it.” This is the only way to give it a deathblow. Are you greedy? Do you feel the world tangling you up? You can struggle against this evil as long as you like, but if it’s the sin that clings to you most, you’ll never be freed from it any other way than by the blood of Jesus. Take it to Christ. Tell him, “Lord, I have trusted thee, and thy name is Jesus, for thou dost save thy people from their sins; Lord, this is one of my sins; save me from it!” Ordinances are nothing without Christ as a means of putting sin to death. Your prayers and your repentances and your tears, all of them put together, are worth nothing apart from him. “None but Jesus can do helpless sinners good”; or helpless saints either. You must be conquerors through him who has loved you, if you’re to be conquerors at all. Our victory wreaths must grow among his olives in Gethsemane.
