modern: Why should our exalted Lord appear in glory with his wounds? The wounds of Jesus are his glories, his jewels, his sacred ornaments. To the believer’s eye, Jesus is exceedingly lovely because he is “white and ruddy”: white with innocence and red with his own blood. We see him as the lily of matchless purity, and as the rose made crimson with his own blood. Christ is lovely on the Mount of Olives and on Tabor and by the sea, but oh, there was never such a matchless Christ as the one who hung on the cross. There we saw all his beauties in perfection, all his attributes displayed, all his love drawn out, all his character expressed. Dear friend, the wounds of Jesus are far lovelier in our eyes than all the splendor and pomp of kings. The crown of thorns is more than an imperial crown. It’s true that he no longer holds the scepter of reed, but there was a glory in it that never flashed from a scepter of gold. Jesus wears the look of a slain Lamb as his court dress, in which he won our souls and redeemed them by his complete atonement. And these aren’t only Christ’s ornaments: they are the *trophies* of his love and of his victory. He has divided the spoil with the strong. He has redeemed for himself a great multitude that no one can number, and these scars are the memorials of the fight. Ah, if Christ loves to keep the memory of his sufferings for his people like this, *how precious his wounds should be to us*!

modern:
There are many times in our experience when we may very rightly, and with benefit, renew our covenant with God. After *recovering from sickness*, when like Hezekiah we’ve had a new term of years added to our life, we may fittingly do it. After any *rescue from trouble*, when our joys bud again, let’s revisit the foot of the cross and renew our dedication. Especially let’s do this after any *sin that has grieved the Holy Spirit* or brought dishonor on the cause of God. Then let’s look to the blood that can make us whiter than snow, and offer ourselves to the Lord again. We shouldn’t only let our troubles confirm our dedication to God; *our prosperity* should do the same. If we ever meet with occasions that deserve to be called “crowning mercies,” then surely, if he has crowned us, we ought to crown our God too. Let’s bring out again all the jewels of the divine regalia stored in the jewel case of our heart, and let our God sit on the throne of our love, dressed in royal robes.

If we learned to profit from our prosperity, we wouldn’t need so much adversity. If we gathered from a kiss all the good it could bring us, we wouldn’t so often smart under the rod. Have we recently received some blessing we hardly expected? Has the Lord set our feet in a wide place? Can we sing of multiplied mercies? Then this is the day to put our hand on the horns of the altar and say, “Bind me here, my God; bind me here with cords, even for ever.” Since we need God to keep new promises to us, let’s offer renewed prayers that our old vows won’t be dishonored. This morning let’s make a sure covenant with him, because of the sufferings of Jesus, which we’ve been thinking about with gratitude for the last month.

modern:
Spring is a sweet season. The long, dreary winter helps us appreciate its kindly warmth, and its promise of summer adds to its present delights. After times of low spirits, it’s delightful to see the light of the Sun of Righteousness again. Then our sleeping graces rise from their sluggishness, like the crocus and the daffodil from their beds of earth. Then our heart is made merry with delicious notes of gratitude, far more musical than the warbling of birds, and the comforting assurance of peace, infinitely more delightful than the turtledove’s call, is heard within the soul. Now is the time for the soul to seek fellowship with her Beloved. Now she must rise from her natural earthiness and come away from her old associations. If we don’t raise the sail when the breeze is favorable, we’ll be to blame. Times of refreshing ought not to pass over us without our making use of them. When Jesus himself visits us tenderly and urges us to rise, can we be so low as to refuse him? He himself has risen, so that he may draw us after him. Now, by his Holy Spirit, he has revived us, so that in newness of life we may go up into the heavenly places and have fellowship with him.

Let our wintry state be enough coldness and indifference for us. When the Lord creates a spring within, let our sap flow strongly and our branch blossom with high resolve. O Lord, if it isn’t springtime in my chilly heart, I pray you, make it so, for I’m thoroughly tired of living at a distance from you. Oh, the long, dreary winter! When will you bring it to an end? Come, Holy Spirit, and renew my soul! Make me alive! Restore me, and have mercy on me! This very night I want to beg the Lord earnestly to take pity on his servant and send me a happy revival of spiritual life!

modern:
Listen, I hear my Beloved’s voice! He’s speaking to *me*! Fair weather is smiling on the face of the earth, and he doesn’t want me spiritually asleep while all nature around me is waking from her winter’s rest. He tells me to “Rise up,” and well he may, for I’ve been lying long enough among the pots of worldliness. He is risen, and I am risen in him; so why should I cling to the dust? I want to rise toward him from lower loves, desires, pursuits and ambitions. He calls me by the sweet name “My love,” and thinks me beautiful; that’s a good reason for me to rise. If he has lifted me up like this and thinks me so lovely, how can I linger in the tents of Kedar and find kindred spirits among the sons of men? He tells me, “Come away.” He calls me further and further from everything selfish, groveling, worldly and sinful; yes, even from the outwardly religious world that doesn’t know him and has no sympathy with the mystery of the higher life. “Come away” doesn’t sound harsh in my ear, for what is there to keep me in this wilderness of emptiness and sin? O my Lord, I wish I could come away, but I’m caught among the thorns and can’t escape them as I’d like to. If it were possible, I’d have no eyes, no ears and no heart for sin.

You call me to yourself by saying, “Come away,” and this is a musical call indeed. To come to you is to come home from exile, to come to land out of the raging storm, to come to rest after long labor, to come to the goal of my desires and the height of my wishes. But Lord, how can a stone rise? How can a lump of clay come away from the horrible pit? Oh, raise me; draw me. Your grace can do it. Send your Holy Spirit to kindle sacred flames of love in my heart, and I’ll keep rising until I leave life and time behind me and really do come away.

modern:
What is your desire this evening? Is it set on heavenly things? Do you long to enjoy the high teaching of eternal love? Do you want freedom in very close fellowship with God? Do you long to know the heights and depths and lengths and breadths? Then you must come near to Jesus. You must get a clear sight of him in his preciousness and completeness. You must see him in his work, in his offices, in his person. Whoever understands Christ receives an anointing from the Holy One, by which he knows all things. Christ is the great master key to all the rooms of God. There’s no treasure house of God that won’t open and give up all its wealth to the soul that lives close to Jesus.

Are you saying, “O that he would dwell in my bosom?” “Would that he would make my heart his dwelling-place for ever?” Open the door, dear friend, and he will come into your soul. He has been knocking a long time, and all with this aim: that he may eat with you, and you with him. *He eats with you* because you provide the house, or the heart; and *you with him* because he brings the food. He couldn’t eat with you if he weren’t in your heart, with you providing the house; and you couldn’t eat with him, since your cupboard is bare, if he didn’t bring food with him. So fling open the gates of your soul. He’ll come with the love you long to feel. He’ll come with the joy you can’t work your poor, low spirit into. He’ll bring the peace you don’t have now. He’ll come with his flagons of wine and sweet apples of love, and cheer you until you have no other sickness but that of “love o’erpowering, love divine.” Only open the door to him, drive out his enemies, give him the keys of your heart, and he’ll live there forever. Oh, wonderful love, that brings such a guest to live in such a heart!

modern:
It seems, then, that Christians can forget Christ! There’d be no need for this loving command if there weren’t a fearful possibility that our memories might prove treacherous. And this isn’t a mere possibility. Sadly, it’s all too well confirmed in our experience, not as something that might happen but as a sorrowful fact. It seems almost impossible that people who have been redeemed by the blood of the dying Lamb, and loved with an everlasting love by the eternal Son of God, should forget that gracious Savior. But startling as it sounds, it’s sadly too plain to see for us to deny the crime. Forget the One who never forgot us! Forget the One who poured out his blood for our sins! Forget the One who loved us even to death! Can it be possible? Yes; it isn’t only possible, but conscience admits it’s all too sadly a fault in every one of us, that we let him be like a traveler who stays only for a night. He whom we should make the permanent resident of our memories is only a visitor there. The cross, where you’d think memory would linger and forgetfulness would be an unknown intruder, is trampled by the feet of forgetfulness.

Doesn’t your conscience say this is true? Don’t you find yourself forgetting Jesus? Some created thing steals your heart away, and you forget the One your love should be set on. Some earthly business takes up your attention when you should fix your eye steadily on the cross. It’s the constant turmoil of the world, the constant pull of earthly things, that draws the soul away from Christ. While memory keeps a poisonous weed all too well, it lets the rose of Sharon wither. Let’s charge ourselves to tie a heavenly forget-me-not around our hearts for Jesus our Beloved, and whatever else we let slip, let’s hold fast to him.

modern:
“We die daily,” said the apostle. This was the life of the early Christians: they went everywhere with their lives in their hands. In our day we aren’t called to go through the same fearful persecutions. If we were, the Lord would give us grace to stand the test. But the tests of Christian life right now, though outwardly not so terrible, are even more likely to overcome us than those of the fiery age. We have to bear the world’s sneer, and that’s small. Its flattery, its soft words, its smooth speeches, its fawning, its hypocrisy are far worse. Our danger is that we’ll grow rich and become proud, that we’ll give ourselves up to the fashions of this present evil world and lose our faith. Or if wealth isn’t the trial, worldly worry is just as harmful. If we can’t be torn to pieces by the roaring lion, we may be hugged to death by the bear. The devil cares little which it is, as long as he destroys our love for Christ and our confidence in him. I’m afraid the Christian church is far more likely to lose her integrity in these soft and silken days than in those rougher times.

We must stay awake now, for we’re crossing the Enchanted Ground, and we’re very likely to fall asleep to our own ruin, unless our faith in Jesus is real and our love for Jesus a burning flame. Many in these days of easy profession are likely to turn out to be weeds and not wheat: hypocrites with fair masks on their faces, but not the true-born children of the living God. Christian, don’t think these are times when you can do without watchfulness or holy zeal. You need them more than ever. And may God the eternal Spirit show his almighty power in you, so that you can say in all these softer things, as well as in the rougher ones, “We are more than conquerors through him that loved us.”

modern:
It’s strange how little use we make of the spiritual blessings God gives us, but it’s stranger still how little use we make of God himself. Though he is “our own God,” we turn to him very little and ask very little of him. How seldom we ask the Lord for advice! How often we go about our business without seeking his guidance! In our troubles, how constantly we try to carry our burdens ourselves, instead of throwing them on the Lord so that he can hold us up! It isn’t because we aren’t allowed, for the Lord seems to say, “I am yours, soul; come and use me as you like. You can come freely to my storehouse, and the more often, the more welcome.” It’s our own fault if we don’t make free with the riches of our God. So since you have such a friend, and he invites you, draw on him every day. Never go without while you have a God to go to. Never fear or faint while you have God to help you. Go to your treasure and take whatever you need; everything you could want is there. Learn the divine skill of making God everything to you. He can supply you with everything, or better still, he can be to you in place of everything.

So let me urge you: make use of your God. Use him *in prayer*. Go to him often, because he is *your* God. Oh, will you fail to use so great a privilege? Run to him; tell him all your needs. Use him constantly *by faith*, at all times. If some dark providence has clouded you over, use your God as a “sun.” If some strong enemy has surrounded you, find in the Lord a “shield,” for he is a sun and shield to his people. If you’ve lost your way in the mazes of life, use him as a “guide,” for he will direct you. Whatever you are and wherever you are, remember that God is just *what* you need, and just *where* you need him, and that he can do *all* you need.

modern:
Jesus Christ is no tyrant claiming *divine right*, but he truly and really is the Lord’s anointed! “It hath pleased the Father that in him should all fulness dwell.” God has given him all power and all authority. As the Son of man, he is now head over all things to his church, and he reigns over heaven and earth and hell, with the keys of life and death at his belt. Some princes have liked to call themselves kings by the *will of the people*, and our Lord Jesus Christ certainly is that in his church. If it could be put to the vote whether he should be King in the church, every believing heart would crown him. Oh, that we could crown him more gloriously than we do! We’d count no expense wasted if it could glorify Christ. Suffering would be pleasure and loss would be gain, if by them we could surround his forehead with brighter crowns and make him more glorious in the eyes of men and angels. Yes, he shall reign. Long live the King! All hail to you, King Jesus! Go out, you pure souls who love your Lord; bow at his feet; scatter his way with the lilies of your love and the roses of your gratitude: “Bring forth the royal diadem, and crown him Lord of all.”

What’s more, our Lord Jesus is King in Zion by *right of conquest*. He has taken the hearts of his people by storm, and has killed the enemies who held them in cruel slavery. In the Red Sea of his own blood our Redeemer has drowned the Pharaoh of our sins: shall he not be King in Jeshurun? He has set us free from the iron yoke and heavy curse of the law: shall the Liberator not be crowned? We are his portion, whom he has taken out of the hand of the Amorite with his sword and with his bow: who will snatch his conquest from his hand? All hail, King Jesus! We gladly accept your gentle rule! Rule in our hearts forever, you lovely Prince of Peace.

modern:
Whatever your particular need, you can easily find some promise in the Bible to suit it. Are you faint and feeble because your road is rough and you’re tired? Here’s the promise: “He giveth power to the faint.” When you read a promise like that, take it back to the great Promiser and ask him to keep his own word. Are you seeking Christ and thirsting for closer fellowship with him? This promise shines on you like a star: “Blessed are they that hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled.” Take that promise to the throne continually. Don’t plead anything else, but go to God again and again with this: “Lord, thou hast said it, do as thou hast said.” Are you distressed about sin and weighed down with the heavy load of your wrongdoing? Listen to these words: “I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions, and will no more remember thy sins.” You have no merit of your own to plead for why he should pardon you, but plead his written commitments and he will carry them out.

Are you afraid you won’t be able to hold on to the end, that after having thought yourself a child of God, you’ll turn out to be a castaway? If that’s your state, take this word of grace to the throne and plead it: “The mountains may depart, and the hills may be removed, but the covenant of my love shall not depart from thee.” If you’ve lost the sweet sense of the Savior’s presence and are seeking him with a sorrowful heart, remember the promises: “Return unto me, and I will return unto you”; “For a small moment have I forsaken thee, but with great mercies will I gather thee.” Feast your faith on God’s own word, and whatever your fears or needs, go to the Bank of Faith with your Father’s signed promise, saying, “Remember the word unto thy servant, upon which thou hast caused me to hope.”

modern:
Are there no exceptions? No, not one. Even the favored race is described like this. If the best are so bad, what must the worst be? Come, my heart, consider how much share you have in this universal accusation, and as you consider it, be ready to take the shame on yourself wherever you’ve been guilty. The first charge is *impudence*, or a hard forehead: a lack of holy shame, an unholy boldness in evil. Before my conversion I could sin and feel no remorse, hear about my guilt and still stay unhumbled, and even confess my sin without any inner humbling over it. For a sinner to go to God’s house and pretend to pray to him and praise him shows a brazen face of the worst kind! And sadly, since the day of my new birth I’ve doubted my Lord to his face, grumbled in his presence without blushing, worshiped before him carelessly and sinned without grieving over it. If my forehead weren’t like adamant, harder than flint, I’d have far more holy fear and a far deeper brokenness of spirit. Woe is me: I’m one of the impudent house of Israel.

The second charge is *hardheartedness*, and I mustn’t dare plead innocent here. Once I had nothing but a heart of stone, and although by grace I now have a new heart of flesh, much of my old stubbornness remains. I’m not moved by the death of Jesus as I ought to be. Nor am I moved as I should be by the ruin of my fellow men, the wickedness of the times, my heavenly Father’s discipline and my own failures. Oh, that my heart would melt at the telling of my Savior’s sufferings and death! I wish to God I were rid of this lower millstone within me, this hateful body of death. Blessed be the name of the Lord, the disease isn’t incurable. The Savior’s precious blood is the universal solvent, and it will truly soften me, even me, until my heart melts like wax before the fire.

modern:
The Christian’s path isn’t always bright with sunshine; he has his seasons of darkness and storm. It’s true that God’s Word says, “Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace”; and it’s a great truth that faith is designed to give a person happiness here below as well as bliss above. But experience tells us that if the course of the just is “As the shining light that shineth more and more unto the perfect day,” sometimes *that* light is eclipsed. At certain times clouds cover the believer’s sun, and he walks in darkness and sees no light. There are many who have rejoiced in God’s presence for a time. They basked in the sunshine in the early stages of their Christian life. They walked in the “green pastures” beside the “still waters.” But suddenly they find the glorious sky clouded over. Instead of the land of Goshen they have to walk the sandy desert. In place of sweet waters they find troubled streams, bitter to their taste, and they say, “Surely, if I were a child of God, this would not happen.”

Oh, don’t say that, you who are walking in darkness! The best of God’s saints must drink the wormwood; the dearest of his children must bear the cross. No Christian has enjoyed unbroken prosperity; no believer can always keep his harp off the willows. Perhaps the Lord gave you a smooth, unclouded path at first because you were weak and timid. He tempered the wind to the shorn lamb. But now that you’re stronger in the spiritual life, you must enter on the riper and rougher experience of God’s grown-up children. We need winds and storms to exercise our faith, to tear off the rotten branch of self-reliance, and to root us more firmly in Christ. The day of evil shows us the value of our glorious hope.

modern:
How all-embracing the love of Jesus is! There’s no part of his people’s interests he doesn’t consider, and nothing that concerns their welfare is unimportant to him. He doesn’t only think of you, believer, as an immortal being, but as a mortal being too. Don’t deny it or doubt it: “The very hairs of your head are all numbered.” “The steps of a good man are ordered by the Lord: and he delighteth in his way.” It would be a sad thing for us if this cloak of love didn’t cover all our concerns, for what harm might be done to us in any part of our affairs that didn’t come under our gracious Lord’s inspection! Believer, be sure that the heart of Jesus cares about your smaller affairs. His tender love is so broad that you can go to him about anything, for in all your troubles he is troubled, and as a father pities his children, so he pities you. The smallest concerns of all his saints are carried on the broad chest of the Son of God. Oh, what a heart he has, that takes in not only the persons of his people but also the many and countless concerns of all those persons!

Do you think, Christian, that you can measure the love of Christ? Think what his love has brought you: justification, adoption, sanctification, eternal life! The riches of his goodness are unsearchable; you’ll never be able to count them, or even imagine them. Oh, the breadth of the love of Christ! Shall a love like this have half our hearts? Shall it get a cold love in return? Shall Jesus’ marvelous lovingkindness and tender care meet with only a faint response and a slow acknowledgment? O my soul, tune your harp to a glad song of thanksgiving! Go to your rest rejoicing, for you’re no lonely wanderer, but a much-loved child, watched over, cared for, provided for and defended by your Lord.

modern:
There are grumblers among Christians now, as there were in Israel’s camp long ago. There are those who cry out against God’s painful dealings when the rod falls. They ask, “Why am I thus afflicted? What have I done to be chastened in this manner?” A word with you, grumbler! Why should you grumble at the dealings of your heavenly Father? Can he treat you more harshly than you deserve? Remember what a rebel you once were, and yet he has pardoned you! Surely, if in his wisdom he now sees fit to discipline you, you shouldn’t complain. After all, are you struck as hard as your sins deserve? Think about the corruption in your heart, and then will you wonder that it takes so much of the rod to bring it out? Weigh yourself, and see how much dross is mixed with your gold; and do you think the fire is too hot to burn away as much dross as you have? Doesn’t that proud, rebellious spirit of yours prove that your heart isn’t thoroughly made holy? Aren’t those grumbling words contrary to the holy, submissive nature of God’s children? Isn’t the correction needed?

But if you *will* grumble against the discipline, take care, for it will go hard with grumblers. God always disciplines his children twice if they don’t bear the first stroke patiently. But know one thing: “He doth not afflict willingly, nor grieve the children of men.” All his corrections are sent in love, to purify you and draw you nearer to himself. Surely it must help you bear the discipline with resignation if you can recognize your *Father’s* hand. For “whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons.” “Murmur not as some of them also murmured and were destroyed of the destroyer.”

modern: God’s knowing everything gives no comfort to the ungodly mind, but to the child of God it overflows with comfort. God is always thinking about us. He never turns his mind away from us; he always has us before his eyes. And this is exactly how we’d want it, for it would be dreadful to exist for a moment outside our heavenly Father’s sight. His thoughts are always tender, loving, wise, careful and far-reaching, and they bring us countless benefits, so it’s a choice delight to remember them. The Lord always did think about his people: hence their election, and the covenant of grace by which their salvation is made sure. He always will think about them: hence their final perseverance, by which they will be brought safely to their final rest. In all our wanderings, the watchful glance of the Eternal Watcher is always fixed on us; we never roam beyond the Shepherd’s eye. In our sorrows he watches us without ceasing, and not a pang escapes him. In our labors he notices all our weariness, and writes down in his book all the struggles of his faithful ones. These thoughts of the Lord surround us in all our paths and reach into the innermost part of our being. Not a nerve or tissue, valve or vessel of our bodies goes uncared for. All the little things of our little world are thought about by the great God.

Dear reader, is this precious to you? Then hold on to it. Never be led astray by those philosophical fools who preach an impersonal God and talk about matter that exists on its own and runs itself. The Lord lives and thinks about us; this truth is far too precious for us to be lightly robbed of it. The notice of a nobleman is valued so highly that whoever has it thinks his fortune made; but what is it to be thought of by the King of kings! If the Lord thinks about us, all is well, and we may rejoice forever.
